analysis.one_liner: Requires every American to enroll in federally approved health insurance, funded partly by higher tobacco and liquor taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, was referred to six House committees without a hearing or vote, and in August 1994 the record simply points to H.R. 3600, which also died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every legal U.S. resident to enroll in a federally approved health insurance policy, with a single national premium set by a new Federal Health Board, full premium subsidies for people below the poverty line, and a sliding scale above it. It would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, military dependents' coverage, and the federal employees' plan, financed in part by roughly tripling the cigarette tax and nearly quadrupling the distilled spirits tax, and would have created a board empowered to revoke the patent of any prescription drug priced excessively.
analysis.who_benefits: All Americans gain guaranteed coverage, including the 33 million the bill's findings say lack basic health services at any given time. Low-income families pay nothing until income reaches the poverty line, then face a gradually shrinking subsidy; enrolled members of federally recognized tribes pay nothing. Patients gain coverage that travels with them anywhere in the country, standardized claim forms, and a consumer's guide to drug prices. Doctors gain relief from malpractice exposure: punitive damages are barred and practitioners' associations, not individuals, pay malpractice judgments.

how_it_helps.text: Every legal resident must be enrolled in an approved policy; states must randomly assign people who fail to enroll, so coverage is universal by default.

Families at or below the federal poverty line get a 100% premium reduction, sliding up to a full-fee income of roughly ten units above poverty (about $10,000 above the poverty line for a family of four); Native Americans enrolled in federally recognized tribes pay nothing.

The bill's findings state that at least 33 million Americans lack access to basic health services at any point in time and that about a quarter of the non-elderly population goes without coverage during any two-year period.
Approved policies must cover all necessary and appropriate practitioner services anywhere in the United States, and premiums may not vary by health status beyond Board-approved rates.
A Prescription Drug Price Review Board would determine whether drug prices or increases are excessive, and could revoke a manufacturer's patent if it refuses to bring the price down.
Providers are insulated from malpractice risk: punitive damages are prohibited and damages are assessed against the practitioners' association rather than the individual practitioner.

analysis.who_pays: Premium payers and taxpayers finance the system: the federal government pays states per capita amounts for district services and reimburses insurers for low-income premium reductions, while states must raise their share through taxes. Smokers and drinkers bear sharply higher excise taxes — the cigarette tax rises from $12 to $30.50 per thousand and the distilled spirits tax from $13.50 to $50.00 — with the proceeds dedicated to a health education trust fund. Brand-name drug makers face federal price review backed by possible patent revocation. Patients lose the ability to sue individual providers punitively for malpractice.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals Medicare, Medicaid, CHAMPUS, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program effective October 1, 1998, replacing them with an untested system of state boards, district global budgets, and Board-approved policies — a disruptive transition for the tens of millions then covered by those programs.
The excise tax increases are steep and regressive: the cigarette tax more than doubles and the liquor tax nearly quadruples, costs passed on to consumers regardless of income.
All legal residents are compelled to enroll, and a state must randomly assign anyone who fails to enroll into a policy — a mandate on individuals, not just on government.

The bill exempts hospitals, nursing homes, and other health entities contracting with state boards from federal and state antitrust laws, removing competition oversight at the same time providers are handed fixed global budgets.

A good-faith objection: fixed global budgets and fee schedules, as in systems like Canada's, can mean waits and limited access to certain services; the bill acknowledges this trade-off by allowing separate private insurance only for services not covered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core promise — universal coverage at a per-capita cost set by global budgets rather than fee-for-service growth — addressed what its own findings describe as the highest health spending share of any industrialized nation combined with tens of millions uninsured. The costs are real: a forced transition off Medicare and Medicaid in five years, a heavier regressive excise tax burden, an individual mandate, and an antitrust exemption for providers that removes a check on the very boards and entities the bill creates. On paper it is a serious, fully specified alternative, but its fate was decided in committee, not on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors, split among six committees and nine subcommittees, never got a hearing or vote, and in August 1994 the record points to H.R. 3600 — the larger Democratic reform bill, which also died before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Collin Peterson of Minnesota introduced the bill on July 13, 1993, and it was referred jointly to six House committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Armed Services, and Post Office and Civil Service.
It attracted no cosponsors at any point.
Between July and August 1993 it was referred to subcommittees in the various committees and the Defense Department was asked for comment; no hearing, markup, or floor action appears in the record.
On August 2, 1994, the final action reads simply 'See H.R. 3600', the broader Democratic leadership health reform bill of that Congress.
H.R. 3600 also never received a House floor vote, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with neither bill enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The industries the bill would have constrained are better off that it never moved: health insurers keep the existing employer-based and Medicare/Medicaid markets instead of a Board-set single premium, and drug makers avoid a price review board armed with patent revocation. Providers avoid global budgets and fee schedules. Members of Congress who preferred other vehicles — or no reform — avoided a vote on a fully specified single-premium system.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and it was never voted on, so no party breakdown of support or opposition exists in the record; the broader Democratic health reform push of 1993-94 also failed to reach a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill makes private insurers the permanent delivery channel: every legal resident must enroll in a Board-approved private policy, with federal premium subsidies paid to the issuers. In exchange, insurers lose pricing freedom — a single national premium per enrollment category, standardized forms, mandatory acceptance of fee schedules — and Medicare, Medicaid, and FEHBP, their biggest public-program counterparts, are repealed.

A new Prescription Drug Price Review Board would rule on whether prices or increases are excessive and could revoke a manufacturer's patent if the price is not lowered. This directly attacks the industry's patent-protected pricing power, which is what high U.S. drug prices are built on.

The cigarette tax more than doubles ($12 to $30.50 per thousand) and the distilled spirits tax nearly quadruples ($13.50 to $50.00), with the revenue dedicated to health education and training. Consumers who smoke or drink pay the tax directly; the industries lose sales volume.

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other care facilities
industries.note: They lose fee-for-service Medicare and Medicaid billing but gain guaranteed district global budgets financed by federal per capita payments — and the bill exempts them from antitrust laws when contracting with state boards, shielding consolidation from competition review.

Practitioners must accept fee-schedule amounts as payment in full, set through their state-chartered associations — which are also exempted from antitrust laws, allowing collective fee bargaining. Malpractice exposure shifts to the association and punitive damages are barred.

State-chartered practitioners' associations take over providing malpractice coverage and paying judgments (directly or by contracting with insurers), and punitive damages are abolished, shrinking the market and risk.
